title: FloatConverter breaks for values smaller than 0.0001
body:
`FloatConverter` uses scientific notation (`1e-05`) when building URLs with values smaller than 0.0001. This leads to URLs, that can not be resolved, as `FloatConverter` does not handle values containing letters (regex: `\d+\.\d+`).

The following listing illustrates the issue:

```python
from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule
from werkzeug.routing.converters import FloatConverter
import typing as t

map = Map([
    Rule('/<float:x>', endpoint='foo'),
])
mapAdapter = map.bind('bar')

print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 1}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 0.00001}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := '/0.00001', mapAdapter.test(url))
```

This leads to the following output:

```
/1.0 True
/1e-05 False
/0.00001 True
```

In the second row, the generated URL can not be resolved. 

There are multiple ways to fix this issue.  One could for example adjust the regex to handle these cases (`\d+\.\d+(e[+-]/d+)?` instead of `\d+\.\d+`). Another option would be to suppress scientific notation when building URLs:

```python
class FixedFloatConverter(FloatConverter):
    def to_url(self, value: t.Any) -> str:
        return f'{self.num_convert(value):f}'
    
map = Map([
    Rule('/<ffloat:x>', endpoint='foo'),
], converters={'ffloat': FixedFloatConverter})
mapAdapter = map.bind('bar')

print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 1}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 0.00001}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := '/0.00001', mapAdapter.test(url))
```

This produces the desired result:

```
/1.000000 True
/0.000010 True
/0.00001 True
```

Environment:

- Python version: not relevant
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.7

When a WWWAuthenticate header with no realm or other parameter is converted to a response header, the header contains an invalid trailing white-space.

Such parameter-less headers are standard: https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#challenge.and.response

Simple reproduction steps:
```py
wa = WWWAuthenticate('bearer')
assert wa.to_header() == "Bearer"  # must not be "Bearer "
```

title: MultiDict does not handle None values
body:
The following code will result in a `TypeError`:
```python
invalid_values = MultiDict([('a', 'x'), ('b', ''), ('d', None)])
print(invalid_values.get('a', type=int))  # None
print(invalid_values.get('b', type=int))  # None
print(invalid_values.get('c', type=int))  # None
print(invalid_values.get('d', type=int))  # TypeError
```
I think the expected behavior would be to return `None` as all other error cases do.

This happens because the following code only checks for `ValueError` and not other errors like `TypeError`:
https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/d3dd65a27388fbd39d146caacf2563639ba622f0/src/werkzeug/datastructures/structures.py#L81-L84

title: Extra Newline Added to Binary File Upload
body:
## Problem:
After uploading a specific binary file, an unexpected newline character (\n) is being added to the beginning of the file. This behavior is traced back to Werkzeug's multipart request body parsing during POST requests.

## Steps to Reproduce:

1. Create a binary file named one_newline_bigger_than_64k with the following content:
```py
with open("one_newline_bigger_than_64k", "wb") as file:
    bytes_to_write = b'X' + b'\n' + 64 * 1024 * b'c'
    file.write(bytes_to_write)
```
2. Upload the one_newline_bigger_than_64k file.
3. Compare the binary content of the original and uploaded files.
## Root Cause:
This issue arises due to Werkzeug's [_parse_data](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/main/src/werkzeug/sansio/multipart.py#L246) method. Specifically, when a newline (\n or \r) is present at the second position (index 1) of the file's content and no additional newlines are within the first 64KB of the request body, an extra newline is inadvertently introduced during parsing.

## Code Flow:

1. Werkzeug's next_event method invokes _parse_data.
2. In _parse_data, a data_start value is set based on the file's content type.
3. If the boundary indicator is absent in the buffer, the [last_newline](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/main/src/werkzeug/sansio/multipart.py#L124) method is employed to locate the latest newline (\n or \r) character in the file's content. However, this method operates on a modified data slice that starts at data_start.
4. Since data is modified, any index from last_newline needs data_start adjustment.
5. Incorrectly adjusted indices lead to an empty byte segment when slicing data[data_start:data_end], resulting in an empty data segment.
6. This leads to an unintended addition of a newline character in the file's content.
## Solution:
To resolve this, a correction in the _parse_data method is needed. The index returned by last_newline should be adjusted by adding the data_start before slicing data.

### Proposed Fix:
Update _parse_data as follows:

```py
# Inside _parse_data method
if self.buffer.find(b"--" + self.boundary) == -1:
    # No complete boundary in buffer, but a partial boundary might exist. 
    # Find the earliest newline (nl or cr) and return data up to that.
    last_newline_idx = self.last_newline(data[data_start:])
    data_end = del_index = last_newline_idx + data_start  # Adjusted index
    more_data = True
```

## Environment:

Python: 3.10.12
Werkzeug: 2.3.6

## Resolution:
A pull request will be created to implement this fix, preventing unintended newline addition in binary file uploads. This adjustment ensures proper index handling, preventing unintended manipulation of file content during parsing.

title: MIMEAccept doesn't respect specificity
body:
Hello!

I've been using the helpful MIMEAccept class in `werkzeug.datastructures` and I noticed that while it does respect quality, it doesn't respect specificity as outlined in RFC 2616.

> Media ranges can be overridden by more specific media ranges or specific media types. If more than one media range applies to a given type, the most specific reference has precedence. For example,
> 
> Accept: text/_, text/html, text/html;level=1, */_
>     have the following precedence:
> 
> 1) text/html;level=1
> 2) text/html
> 3) text/*
> 4) */*

Is this something that people are interested in seeing fixed? I'd be happy to open a pull.

title: url parameters casting bytes to str
body:
Hi there! I noticed a change in behavior in werkzeug 0.15.x whereby url parameters used to be safe to send as bytes (on python 3.6).

I apologize for not showing a more direct example in werkzeug, but like most users of werkzeug - I don't use it directly - I use it through flask.

Demonstration (using Flask)

```python
from flask import Flask, url_for

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config['SERVER_NAME'] = 'www.foo.com'


@app.route('/<string:foo>')
def hello(foo):
    return 'Hello, World!'


with app.app_context():
    print(url_for('hello', foo=b'bar'))
```

With `werkzeug<0.15`, this will output:

```
http://www.foo.com/bar
```

However as of `werkzeug>=0.15`, it now returns this malformed url:

```
http://www.foo.com/b%27bar%27
```

I would expect that if `werkzeug` isn't going to decode bytes for you anymore, that it ought to raise a `TypeError` indicating that `bytes` is no longer safe to pass in.

I hope this example makes sense! Thanks for reviewing my issue - I'd be happy to (attempt to) submit a pull request if y'all agree that this is not desirable behavior.

title: WSGIRequestHandler should be able to process multiple accept header with same field name.
body:
From https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec4.html section 4.2 last paragraph it should be possible to combine the multiple headers fields.

The way it is currently implemented it takes into account just one accept header https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/serving.py#L138

example of a request sent by docker client:
```
Host: localhost:5001
User-Agent: docker/1.10.3 go/go1.6.3 kernel/4.6.7-300.fc24.x86_64 os/linux arch/amd64
Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json
Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v1+prettyjws
Accept: application/json
Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json
Accept-Encoding: gzip
Connection: close
```
As you can see it sends multiple accept headers.

And this is what we get after headers get processed:

```
'HTTP_ACCEPT': 'application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json'
```

`Expected behaviour`

Other accept headers got lost. It should be possible to combine multiple header fields into one, so eventually we would contain a comma separated list of all accept headers.
Something like:
```
HTTP_ACCEPT': 'application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json, application/json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v1+prettyjws'
```

title: TypeError in BaseRequest.trusted_hosts when a host name starts with a '.'
body:
Adding a host name starting with `.` to `wrappers.BaseRequest.trusted_hosts` results in `TypeError: must be str, not bytes` (Python 3.6) or `TypeError: Can't convert 'bytes' object to str implicitly` (Python 3.4), as in `werkzeug.wsgi.host_is_trusted`, `_normalize` first calls `_encode_idna`, which encodes the `ref` to `bytes` and then if it start with '.', [it is concatenated with the `'.'`](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/0644c6263b1b3b6705426782c1b39a15e04450af/werkzeug/wsgi.py#L133), thus mixing `str` and `bytes`.

## Sample App

```python
from flask import Flask, request

class TrustedHosts:
    """Flask extension setting `werkzeug.wrappers.BaseRequest.trusted_hosts`."""
    def __init__(self, app=None, trusted_hosts=None):
        self.app = app
        self.trusted_hosts = trusted_hosts
        if app is not None:
            self.init_app(app)

    def init_app(self, app):
        app.before_request(self.set_trusted_hosts)

    def set_trusted_hosts(self):
        # As host is a @cached_property this should before its first access.
        request.trusted_hosts = self.trusted_hosts
        print(request.host)

app = Flask(__name__)
```

title: Response.calculate_content_length doesn't use encoded self.response
body:
The implementation of `calculate_content_length` doesn't encode the elements of `self.response` before using them:
https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/wrappers.py#L926

``` python
    def calculate_content_length(self):
        [...]
        return sum(len(x) for x in self.response)
```

In case self.response is composed of utf-8 encoded unicode strings, this will lead to an  invalid return length:

``` python
>>> from werkzeug import Response
>>> r = Response()
>>> r.response.append(u'你好')
>>> r.calculate_content_length()
2
>>> len(u'你好'.encode('utf-8'))
6
```

The easier solution to this would be to use `iter_encoded` inside `calculate_content_length`, but would decrease performances given the data would be encoded two time (for calculating content-lenght, then for actualy writing the data)

Environment:

```
Flask==0.10.1
Werkzeug==0.9.1
```

Test case:

``` py
#/usr/bin/env python2.7
from flask import Flask, Response

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/')
def root():
    resp = Response()
    resp.age = 42
    return resp

if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = app.test_client()
    resp = client.get('/')

    print "Age header:", resp.headers['Age']
```

```
Age header: Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:42 GMT
```

[The HTTP spec says (in part; emphasis added):](http://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec14.html)

> The Age response-header field conveys the sender's estimate of the **amount of time** since the response (or its revalidation) was generated at the origin server.
> `age-value = delta-seconds`
> Age values are **non-negative decimal integers**, representing time in seconds.

body:
If a client sends a bad content type such as `` `or` , `Werkzeug will throw a`ValueError`` exception. 

**Minimal failing example**

``` python
>>> from io import BytesIO
>>> from werkzeug import wrappers
>>> data = 'test'
>>> request = wrappers.Request.from_values(
...     input_stream=BytesIO(data),
...     content_length=len(data),
...     content_type=' , ',
...     method='POST'
... )
>>> request.form
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "werkzeug/utils.py", line 73, in __get__
    value = self.func(obj)
  File "werkzeug/wrappers.py", line 492, in form
    self._load_form_data()
  File "werkzeug/wrappers.py", line 358, in _load_form_data
    mimetype, options = parse_options_header(content_type)
ValueError: need more than 0 values to unpack
```

**Problem:**
[http.parse_options_header](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/http.py#L325) can return an empty tuple, however [Request._load_form_data](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/wrappers.py#L358) always expect it to return a two-tuple:

The ValueError will result in an Internal Server Error being send to the client, when in fact I think it would be more appropriate to reply with 400 Bad Request.

title: Add an 'extras_require' entry to setup.py for watchdog
body:
The reloader feature has an optional dependency on the watchdog package:
http://werkzeug.pocoo.org/docs/0.11/serving/#reloader

Whilst people can just add 'watchdog' to their requirements files, it's clearer to specifically add an `extras_require` entry for it to setup.py, which allows people to instead add eg `Werkzeug[watchdog]` to their requirements file, which more clearly shows why the dependency is required.

In addition, should Werkzeug ever need a specific version of watchdog in the future (eg due to backwards incompatibilities), then the `extras_require` entry could be updated with a version range, causing zero breakage for people who'd used the `Werkzeug[watchdog]` form in their requirements file.

I'll open a PR for this shortly :-)

title: Writing to response.stream does not invalidate/reset Content-Length
body:
This is mostly an issue for "expensive" stream (e.g. images from disk resized on the fly), as the request's conditionality check will likely be performed before computing the payload, at least when it comes to `last_modified`/`if-modified-since`: the conditional response check is performed via `make_conditional` which will [compute a Content-Length if none is present](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/wrappers.py#L1406)[0].

With an empty response (body not computed/set yet) this yields a `Content-Length` of 0. If one then uses `set_data`, by default (with `automatically_set_content_length=True`) it [will re-compute and re-set the `Content-Length` header](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/wrappers.py#L903) whereas [`ResponseStream.write` will neither invalidate nor recompute an existing `Content-Lenght`](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/wrappers.py#L1487).

As a result, if `make_conditional` was called before setting the response's content and the response's content was set using `response.stream` (e.g. by passing it to pillow's `image.save`) the browser will get a `Content-Length` of `0` and will thus ignore all content.

[0] Also note that it does not check for the `automatically_set_content_length` flag. Not an issue here, but still...

title: www-authenticate qop= is not quoted
body:
According to http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2617#section-3.2.1 the `qop` attribute of the `www-authenticate` header is always enquoted even when a single token.

But `werkzeug.WWWAuthenticate` leaves it unquoted when it is a single token:

``` python
>>> foo = werkzeug.Response()
>>> foo.www_authenticate.set_digest('REALM','NONCE',qop=("auth","auth-int"))
>>> print foo.headers['WWW-Authenticate']
Digest nonce="NONCE", realm="REALM", qop="auth, auth-int"
>>> foo.www_authenticate.set_digest('REALM','NONCE',qop=("auth",))
>>> print foo.headers['WWW-Authenticate']
Digest nonce="NONCE", realm="REALM", qop=auth
```

Some clients may be happy with this, but others surely are not.

To correct it I believe it is sufficent to add `'qop'` to `WWWAuthenticate._require_quoting`.

title: Generated SSL cert is too old for Firefox 33+
body:
So with version 33, Firefox did something rather annoying, they now use a more restrictive library that rejects connections to servers running older versions of SSL.  On the one hand, this is pretty awesome because at some point we all need to grow up and start using modern encryption, but on the other, it can make development _really_ difficult when all you really need a an SSL setup -- _any_ SSL setup to make your local development environment Just Work.

We've been using [django-extenstion's](http://django-extensions.readthedocs.org/en/latest/) `runserver_plus` feature, which is awesome because it includes a browser-based debugger and other really cool stuff, but also importantly, it supports the ability for you to run the Django `runserver` in SSL mode.  This means that you can do stuff like:

```
./manage.py runserver_plus --cert=/tmp/temporary.cert
```

And that's enough for you to be able to access your site over SSL:

```
https://localhost:8000/
```

However, now that Firefox has thrown this monkeywrench into things, we spent far too much time today trying to figure out what was wrong and how to fix it, so I'm posting the answer here:

**Basically, you just need a better cert than the one `django-extensions` creates for you automatically.**

So, instead of just running `--cert=/path/to/file` and letting `runserver_plus` create it for you, you should run `openssl` yourself to create the cert and then point `runserver_plus` to it:

```
$ openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout /tmp/temporary-cert.key -out /tmp/temporary-cert.crt
$ ./manage.py runserver_plus --cert=/tmp/temporary-cert.crt
```

Of course, you can locate `temporary-cert.*` wherever you like, but you get the idea.

There's a [Reddit discussion](http://www.reddit.com/r/django/comments/2jbs45/django_runserver_plus_with_ssl_and_firefox_33/) on this as well if you're interested.

title: (Slightly) wrong exception raised for `abort(400)`
body:
Calling `abort(400)` raises `ClientDisconnected`, a sub-class of `BadRequest`, instead of raising `BadRequest` as expected. Users that `try`/`except` for `BadRequest` won't notice the bug, since it is a sub-class; but if you are logging exceptions, the log lines are misleading.

Here's a trivial REPL session that demonstrates the issue:

``` python
>>> import werkzeug
>>> werkzeug.__version__
'0.9.4'
>>> from werkzeug.exceptions import abort, ClientDisconnected
>>> try:
...     abort(400)
... except ClientDisconnected:
...     print "GOT WRONG EXCEPTION"
... except Exception, e:
...     print "Got %r" % e
...
GOT WRONG EXCEPTION
>>>
```

This seems to be due to https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/exceptions.py#L542-L549 -- the sub-class will inherit the parent class's `code` attribute. So technically, this bug is non-deterministic, since it depends on the iteration order of `globals()`.

title: Use mock for testing cache expiration?
body:
I needed to test cache expiration in my application, so I thought "let's see how they did it in werkzeug" :)

By looking at the test suite, I spotted this:

https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/testsuite/contrib/cache.py#L85

but I'm not 100% sure I like that approach, since, although very simple, it has some drawbacks due to the need of waiting for the cache to expire:
- The test requires at least a second to run. This can be the problem should we need to perform many of such tests
- Attempting to use that approach with longer times would make tests take unnecessarily long times to run

So, I ended up using mock to fake the date seen by the cache module:

``` python
    import time
    import mock
    now = time.time()

    def fake_date(delta=0):
        return mock.patch(
            'werkzeug.contrib.cache.time',
            return_value=(now + delta))

    with fake_date(0):
        myfunc(4)  # This is a cached function, with 30s timeout
        assert calls['myfunc'] == 1  # that has a decorator to count calls :)

    with fake_date(10):
        myfunc(4)
        assert calls['myfunc'] == 1

    with fake_date(60):
        myfunc(4)
        assert calls['myfunc'] == 2
```

I'm reporting what I did here because:
- it might be worth using in the werkzeug test
- or, my approach may be bad for some reason I couldn't spot, and I'd like to hear about :)

title: werkzeug.useragents parses IE11 default user agent strings incorrectly
body:
werkzeug.useragents import UserAgent, will parse the default IE 11 user agent string browser as seamonkey.

See http://blogs.msdn.com/b/ieinternals/archive/2013/09/21/internet-explorer-11-user-agent-string-ua-string-sniffing-compatibility-with-gecko-webkit.aspx here for examples of the default IE11 user agent string.

title: CombinedMultiDict can't be converted to bool
body:
During check if `CombinedMultiDict` is `True` the following code is being executed:

```
def __len__(self):
    return len(self.keys())
```

TypeError is being raised:

```
TypeError: object of type 'set_iterator' has no len()
```

Easy to reproduce using flask by executing:

```
bool(request.values)
```

The above code works well with `MultiDict`:

```
bool(request.args)
```

title: session example not working
body:
Example "examples/contrib/sessions.py" doesn't work for me.

I note that SessionMiddleware in werkzeug/contrib/sessions.py doesn't save the session if it is new, so I had to modified it:

diff git/werkzeug/werkzeug/contrib/sessions.py  sessions.py
339c339  
 <             if session.should_save:                                                                                                 

---

> ```
>         if session.should_save or session.new:  
> ```

I note this problem in other examples on internet: new sessions are marked as "new" but not as "modified", but the saving check is made only on the "should_save" attibute.
Probably some default values is changed during last years.

title: Stop escaping non-reserved characters in URLs
body:
Currently, only alphanumeric characters plus "_.-" are marked as always safe. As defined in [URL RFC 1738](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc1738.txt) a few more characters are allowed and thus should be included in _always_safe in urls.py.

> Thus, only alphanumerics, the special characters "$-_.+!*'(),", and reserved characters used for their reserved purposes may be used unencoded within a URL.

title: X-Forwarded-Host may contain commas
body:
Hi,

At work, we recently switched to a set up with an Apache mod_proxy at the edge of our network and then another mod_proxy local to the machine one of our applications is hosted on. This lead to us getting this header back from a Flask app:

`Location: http://vooadmin.temp.iweb.co.uk, vooadmin.temp.iweb.co.uk/users/login`

And we traced this back to the X-Forwarded-Host header which, when using two Apache mod_proxy instances, can be comma separated. The Django guys had this 5 years ago: https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/9064 but their solution was to remove support for trusting this header.

In our app we just used `RequestHeader unset X-Forwarded-Host` in Apache as a work around, but the default behaviour in Werkzeug could probably be improved to just use the first entry if it's comma separated.

Aaron

title: Provide a built-in development server command-line interface.
body:
As discussed on the mailing list:
http://flask.pocoo.org/mailinglist/archive/2011/7/22/application-mount-point/#abdbeee9ca8eda65f0e17a0aeb4fab5f

Make it possible to run a Flask application from the command line with this:

```
$ python -mflask.server yourapplication
```

What would that do?  It would attempt to import yourapplication and then looks for an object called "app".  If it finds that it uses that, otherwise you would have to do (yourapplication:application) or something.  Then it runs that with the development server.

What would that solve?

First of all it would no longer require `if __name__ == '__main__'`, secondly it would solve the double importing problems we commonly see as well as the fact that modules work different to applications.  Lastly the application object would no longer have to be a Flask application object but just any WSGI application object.

title: Storing True and False in a RedisCache is broken
body:
Just recently got burned by improper deserialization of False in RedisCache.  in `dump_object`, `False` gets serialized to `'False'` due to bool being a subclass of int.  However, in `load_object`, `int('False')` raises an error, because False can't be cast to an int.  This is mainly a problem when checking for false, as `'True'` evaluates with an affirmative truth value.

Here's a test highlighting the issue:

```
# werkzeug/testsuite/contrib/cache.py
def test_true_false(self):
  c = self.make_cache()
  c.set('foo', True)
  assert c.get('foo') == True

  c.set('bar', False)
  assert c.get('bar') == False
```

title: Fixing Mistakes as long as we can, Unicode Edition
body:
Right now Werkzeug uses the ignore error handling for incoming unicode data. This was a mistake, it should have been replace. The reason for that is that it's hard to spot if things are removed because of improper encoding.

While this is a backwards incompatible change it still should be done.

The other problem is that Werkzeug supports a fallback:charset error handling. This instead should have been implemented with the help of the codecs module as an optional error handler that can be registered.

title: is_resource_modified() gotcha when datetime has microseconds
body:
When last_modified has a non-zero microseconds component, is_resource_modified() will almost always return true under normal circumstances. HTTP dates don't store microseconds, so the incoming If-Modified-Since header will be parsed into a datetime object with 0 as its microseconds component, and compared against a last_modified value which is slightly larger.

A simple solution would be to do `last_modified = last_modified.replace(microsecond=0)` in is_resource_modified(), although I guess that could occasionally break applications that really do change resources more than once per second. This should at least be documented as a gotcha, I think.

title: Redirect double quoting
body:
Hi everyone,

as my colleague posted on the tipfy dev list, there is a bug in Werkzeug.urls.redirect that ends up double quoting the location-headers. That function calls iri_to_uri in case the location is a unicode object. As of the today this is not only not necessary anymore as it will be done in Response.get_wsgi_headers anyway[1], it even causes harm. It is caused by the fact that werkzeug.utils.iri_to_uri might return a unicode and sets that as the location header and get_wsgi_header is quoting it again.

Removing those two lines in url.redirect is an easy and necessary fix for it. The work-a-round for now is to ensure you pass an quoted non-unicode-object as the location to the function.

[1] https://github.com/mitsuhiko/werkzeug/blob/master/werkzeug/wrappers.py#L951

title: werkzeug.Href behaves strange for names with colons
body:
When joining stuff, unexpected URLs happen if joined name has a colon inside:

```
>>> import werkzeug as w
>>> h = w.Href('/')
>>> h('foo')
'/foo'                        <--- ok
>>> h('foo:bar')
'foo:bar'                     <--- resulting in browser trying wrong protocol
>>> h('a&o')
'/a%26o'                      <--- ok
>>> h(u'übel')
'/%C3%BCbel'                  <--- ok
```

Armin found that this is probably a side effect of using urljoin, that it should be fixed either in werkzeug or stdlib and proposed this workaround:

```
>>> urlparse.urljoin('/', 'foo:bar')
'foo:bar'
>>> urlparse.urljoin('/', './foo:bar')
'/foo:bar'
```

body:

title: werkzeug.contrib.fixers.ProxyFix is not safe under common proxy situations
body:
ProxyFix parses the X-Forwarded-For header to find out the "real" IP address for apps that are deployed behing a proxy (e.g. Heroku, Webfaction, Nginx, CloudFlare, Varnish). But in the default configuration of all these proxies/services, it is trivial for a client to spoof their IP address to any arbitrary string.

Perhaps easier to show than tell. Here's a simple app using ProxyFix deployed to Heroku (source here https://github.com/elidickinson/flask-proxy-demo)

$ curl http://flask-proxy-demo.herokuapp.com/
Your IP address is 68.55.214.2  ( <-- it works, that's me!)

$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4" http://flask-proxy-demo.herokuapp.com/
Your IP address is 1.2.3.4

$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: <script>alert(1)" http://flask-proxy-demo.herokuapp.com/
Your IP address is <script>alert(1)

This would not be a problem if your proxy server (or first proxy server if you have multiple layers) is configured to strip out existing X-Forwarded-For headers on incoming requests rather than append to them. But AFAIK this is not the default on any common proxy and I don't think it's even really possible on Heroku or Webfaction or similar services where the proxy isn't under your control.

ProxyFix's approach of picking the _first_ X-Forwarded-For address is not a good default. I could think of many other ways to do this that would be safer. The obvious solution would be to change ProxyFix to select the _last_ IP in X-Forwarded-For instead. Not perfect, but I think it's a much saner default.

title: Python 3 port available for testing and review
body:
I have a preliminary single source python 2.7/3.3 port of Werkzeug in my tree:
https://github.com/benselme/werkzeug/tree/python3
- So far the testsuite runs successfully in both Python versions: the 261 tests pass. 
- The most basic examples run in the local server, including in debugging mode.

This is just a first step of course, there's going to be a lot of work testing all this in all the envrionments that werkzeug supports, so help in the usual form of bug reports and pull requests is very welcome.

A word about how it was done... Six was used to maintain compatibility using just one version of the sources. Besides striving to be PEP3333 compliant, the idea is that the API should still accept str everywhere whatever the version of Python used. Of course, that means bytes in 2.7 and unicode in 3.3, so there are conversions going on in a lot of places, especially where bytes are needed. There will certainly be a performance hit from this but I'm not sure there's way around that. On the other hand, this should reduce the amount of work needed to port apps that use werkzeug.

Anyway, waiting for your comments ! - Béranger
